column2: Digoxin effect is down-sloping ('reverse tick') ST depression with T flattening and short QT; toxicity shows as brady/junctional rhythms, ectopics or atrial tachycardia with block.
Hypertension is the commonest condition underlying AF (atrial pressure load); others: IHD, heart failure, valve disease, thyroid, alcohol, obesity, sleep apnoea.
Mobitz I: progressive PR prolongation until a dropped beat; AV-nodal, often benign, rarely needs pacing. Mobitz II (infranodal) progresses and needs pacing.
AF is treated with rate control, rhythm control (cardioversion, drugs, ablation) and anticoagulation. An ICD treats ventricular arrhythmias only.
AF at 120/min with hypertension and IHD: a beta-blocker (metoprolol) controls rate, BP and angina. He also needs a DOAC rather than aspirin.
Fusion beats prove AV dissociation and are diagnostic of VT; collapse means pulseless VT, treated like VF with immediate defibrillation.
A rate of 36/min with P waves independent of QRS is complete heart block; after anterior MI it is infranodal (septal necrosis) and needs pacing.
AF with shock (BP 70/50) needs immediate synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation, with heparin, whatever the AF duration.
CHA2DS2-VASc = 6 (age ≥ 75 ×2, female, HTN, diabetes, HF): long-term anticoagulation, preferably a DOAC (rivaroxaban/apixaban). Antiplatelets are not adequate.
Symptomatic AF despite drugs in an older HF patient: 'pace and ablate' (pacemaker then AV-node ablation) gives permanent rate control; PV isolation is the rhythm option.
Rate control uses beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil or digoxin. Amiodarone is mainly for rhythm control and too toxic for long-term rate control.
CHA2DS2-VASc: heart failure, hypertension, age, diabetes, stroke/TIA, vascular disease, female sex. Obesity raises AF risk but is not in the score.
PR > 200 ms: AV-nodal drugs, hypokalaemia, rheumatic fever, Lyme disease, inferior MI, fibrosis. Hypocalcaemia prolongs the QT, not the PR.
The key complication of AF is ischaemic stroke from left atrial appendage thrombus (risk ×5); hence CHA2DS2-VASc and anticoagulation.
Antipsychotics (risperidone, haloperidol) block hERG channels, prolong QT and cause torsades. Treat with IV magnesium and stop the drug.
Irregular cannon a waves mean AV dissociation (complete heart block, VT); regular ones occur in junctional rhythms. AF abolishes a waves.
Orthodromic AVRT is narrow and AV-node-dependent, so adenosine terminates it. In pre-excited AF (irregular, broad) AV-nodal blockers are dangerous.
Rapid irregular palpitations in an older person are most likely AF (prevalence ~10% over 80); confirm with an ECG during symptoms.
Constant PR with sudden dropped P waves is Mobitz II: infranodal, progresses to complete block and causes Stokes–Adams attacks — permanent pacemaker.
Sick sinus syndrome: sinus bradycardia, pauses, SA block, often with AF/atrial tachycardia (tachy–brady). VT is not a feature.
Age ≥ 75 (2) + female (1) + hypertension (1) + diabetes (1) = 5: high stroke risk; offer a DOAC.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first (modified Valsalva), then adenosine 6–12–18 mg rapid bolus. DC shock if unstable.
Permanent pacing for symptomatic bradycardia (sick sinus with syncope), Mobitz II and complete heart block. Athletes' bradycardia is physiological.
Alcohol triggers AF ('holiday heart') and heavy intake raises AF incidence; abstinence reduces recurrence. It also causes dilated cardiomyopathy.
Heart block plus erythema nodosum suggests sarcoidosis: granulomas in the septum/conduction system; confirm with cardiac MRI or FDG-PET.
Broad QRS with rSR' ('M') in V1–V2 and slurred S in I, aVL, V5–V6 is RBBB. LBBB gives a broad QS in V1 and notched R in V6.
Sinus bradycardia, first-degree and Wenckebach block are physiological in asymptomatic athletes; no tests or restriction needed.
A prolonged sinus node recovery time after overdrive pacing (1800 ms) with low intrinsic rate means intrinsic SA node disease.
Reversible SA node dysfunction: hypothermia, hypothyroidism, raised ICP, drugs, hyperkalaemia, vagal tone. Radiation causes permanent fibrosis.
Tachy–brady syndrome includes AF/flutter; atrial enlargement (and age, prior stroke, LV dysfunction) adds embolic risk. A pacemaker does not remove it.
Decremental conduction (slower conduction at faster rates) is shown by atrial pacing at shorter cycle lengths with a lengthening AH interval until Wenckebach.
The AV node lies near the aortic annulus, so AVR/TAVI can cause complete heart block; pace permanently if it persists beyond ~5–7 days.
Constant PR then sudden dropped P waves with syncope is Mobitz II; it tends to progress to complete block, so implant a permanent pacemaker.
Nocturnal Mobitz I in an asymptomatic athlete is high vagal tone; it resolves with exercise. Reassure.
Monitoring depends on symptom frequency: Holter for daily symptoms, event recorder for every few days, implantable loop recorder for rare episodes.
Atrial premature complexes are common and benign in a normal heart; reassure and reduce caffeine/alcohol. Beta-blocker only if troublesome.
Sudden loss of the delta wave on exercise shows a pathway with a long refractory period, so low risk of pre-excited AF degenerating to VF.
Recent-onset AF converts with DC shock, flecainide or amiodarone. Adenosine only transiently blocks the AV node and does not convert AF.
AF with heart failure, hypertension, vascular disease and age ≥ 75 (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 5): oral anticoagulation is class I. Flecainide is contraindicated.
Rhythm control did not improve survival (AFFIRM) and asymptomatic recurrence is common, so anticoagulation follows CHA2DS2-VASc, not apparent sinus rhythm.
Irregular very fast broad complexes of varying shape are pre-excited AF; with collapse give immediate DC shock. AV-nodal blockers can precipitate VF.
Irregularly irregular broad complexes with varying width and RR < 250 ms is AF conducting down an accessory pathway. VT and AVRT are regular.
A regular broad ventricular rhythm at 60–110/min soon after thrombolysis is accelerated idioventricular rhythm, a benign reperfusion marker.
Torsades from methadone + erythromycin persisting after magnesium: raise the rate with isoprenaline or overdrive pacing to shorten QT. Amiodarone worsens it.
AV dissociation (independent P waves, fusion or capture beats) is diagnostic of VT. Prior MI, QRS > 160 ms and chest-lead concordance also favour VT.
